name: Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type (NPHS1)

reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Oxford Textbook of Medicine
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder from NPHS1 mutations affecting nephrin, a key protein of the glomerular slit diaphragm
It causes massive proteinuria that begins in utero or within the first months of life, defining the congenital nephrotic syndrome
A large placenta at birth and a raised maternal serum and amniotic alpha-fetoprotein are characteristic antenatal clues
Affected infants present with gross oedema, hypoalbuminaemia and heavy proteinuria, often with prematurity and small birth weight
Complications include recurrent infection, thrombosis, poor growth and hypothyroidism from urinary loss of binding proteins
It does not respond to corticosteroids or other immunosuppression, unlike acquired childhood nephrotic syndrome
Supportive management addresses protein and fluid losses, nutrition, infection and thrombosis prevention, progressing toward dialysis and transplantation as kidney function fails
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in NPHS1, encoding nephrin, a transmembrane protein that forms the structural backbone of the glomerular slit diaphragm between podocyte foot processes. Loss of functional nephrin disrupts this size- and charge-selective filtration barrier, so plasma proteins, chiefly albumin, leak massively into the urine from before birth. The resulting hypoalbuminaemia produces severe oedema, while urinary loss of immunoglobulins, anticoagulant and hormone-binding proteins predisposes to infection, thrombosis and endocrine disturbance, and ongoing podocyte injury leads to progressive glomerulosclerosis and kidney failure.
additionalDifferentials: Diffuse mesangial sclerosis (for example NPHS2 or WT1-related disease)
Congenital infections causing secondary nephrotic syndrome (for example syphilis, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis)
Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome of infancy from other podocyte genes
Secondary nephrotic syndrome from maternal systemic disease
additionalInvestigations: Quantification of proteinuria and serum albumin
Maternal and amniotic alpha-fetoprotein and placental weight review
Screening for congenital infection as a secondary cause
Thyroid function and immunoglobulin levels given urinary protein losses
Renal ultrasound and, where needed, biopsy to characterise glomerular changes
Genetic testing of NPHS1 and related podocyte genes with parental carrier assessment
redFlags: Overwhelming infection or sepsis in a hypogammaglobulinaemic infant
Thrombosis, including renal vein thrombosis, from the hypercoagulable state
Severe refractory oedema with respiratory or feeding compromise
Progressive decline toward end-stage kidney disease requiring renal replacement
reference.prognosis: Without intensive supportive care the outlook in infancy is poor, but with modern management of protein losses, nutrition and infection, and progression to dialysis and transplantation, long-term survival is achievable in specialist centres.
pitfalls: Trialling corticosteroids or immunosuppression, which are ineffective in this genetic barrier defect
Overlooking secondary hypothyroidism from urinary loss of thyroxine-binding globulin
Underestimating infection and thrombosis risk from urinary loss of immunoglobulins and anticoagulant proteins
Delaying genetic diagnosis, which is essential for prognosis and family counselling
management: Regular intravenous albumin infusions to control severe oedema and intravascular depletion
High-protein, high-calorie nutrition, often via nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding, to counter urinary protein loss and support growth
Reduce proteinuria pharmacologically with ACE inhibitors and indometacin, and consider unilateral or bilateral nephrectomy for intractable losses
Infection prophylaxis and prompt treatment given immunoglobulin loss, with thromboprophylaxis for the hypercoagulable state
Thyroxine replacement for hypothyroidism from urinary binding-protein loss, plus vitamin D and other supplements
Recognise that it does not respond to corticosteroids or immunosuppression, and plan for dialysis and renal transplantation as kidney failure progresses
Genetic counselling and parental carrier testing for autosomal recessive NPHS1 inheritance
